name: Proof of \olref{prop:rep-id}
text:
If $n = m$, then $
um{n}$ and $
um{m}$ are the same term, and
$\Char{=}(n, m) = 1$. But $\Th{Q} \Proves (\eq[
um{n}][
um{m}] \land
\eq[
um{1}][
um{1}])$, so it proves $!A_=(
um{n}, 
um{m},

um{1})$.  If $n 
eq m$, then $\Char=(n, m) = 0$. By
\olref{lem:q-proves-neq}, $\Th{Q} \Proves \eq/[
um{n}][
um{m}]$ and
so also $(\eq/[
um{n}][
um{m}] \land \Obj 0 = \Obj 0)$. Thus $\Th{Q}
\Proves !A_=(
um{n}, 
um{m}, 
um{0})$.

For the second part, we also have two cases. If $n = m$, we have to
show that $\Th{Q} \Proves \lforall[y][(!A_=(
um{n}, 
um{m}, y)
  \lif \eq[y][
um{1}])]$.  Arguing informally, suppose $!A_=(
um{n},

um{m}, y)$, i.e.,
\[
(\eq[
um{n}][
um{n}] \land \eq[y][
um{1}]) \lor
(\eq/[
um{n}][
um{n}] \land \eq[y][
um{0}])
\]
The left disjunct implies $\eq[y][
um{1}]$ by logic; the right
contradicts $\eq[
um{n}][
um{n}]$ which is provable by logic.

Suppose, on the other hand, that $n 
eq m$. Then $!A_=(
um{n},

um{m}, y)$ is
\[
(\eq[
um{n}][
um{m}] \land \eq[y][
um{1}]) \lor
(\eq/[
um{n}][
um{m}] \land \eq[y][
um{0}])
\]
Here, the left disjunct contradicts $\eq/[
um{n}][
um{m}]$, which is
provable in $\Th{Q}$ by \olref{lem:q-proves-neq}; the right disjunct
entails $\eq[y][
um{0}]$.
